topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition.**

**Playwright** (Microsoft, 2020, Apache-2.0) is a browser automation framework that speaks CDP (Chromium), Juggler (Firefox) and WebKit (WebKit -- the engine Safari uses, on Linux). Its three defining properties are: **auto-waiting** locators, **browser-context isolation** (a fresh context, with its own cookies, storage and permissions, in milliseconds), and **tracing** (a full record of the run: DOM snapshots, screenshots, network, console, timing). Its test runner is a first-class test runner with projects, fixtures, retries, sharding, reporters, and parallelism across browsers.

**Mechanics -- the locator model, which is the whole philosophy.**

A **locator** is a lazy, auto-retrying query. Nothing happens until you act or assert. Each action polls the locator until it is actionable (visible, stable, enabled, receives events) or the timeout expires. This is why a Playwright test with no explicit waits is more reliable than a Selenium test with `sleep`s.

```ts
// The priority order, strongest first.
const byRole       = page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })        // accessible role + name
const byLabel      = page.getByLabel('Email address')                          // form control label
const byPlaceholder = page.getByPlaceholder('Search products')                  // weakest text-ish
const byText       = page.getByText('Order confirmed')                          // static text
const byAlt        = page.getByAltText('Company logo')                          // image
const byTestId     = page.getByTestId('order-total')                           // last resort
const byCss        = page.locator('.btn-primary')                               // almost always wrong
const byXpath      = page.locator('xpath=//div[contains(@class,"btn")]')        // almost always wrong

// Chaining, scoping, and filtering -- the power features.
await page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Ada Lovelace' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit' }).click()
await page.locator('article').filter({ has: page.getByRole('img', { name: 'broken' }) }).count()
await page.getByRole('listitem').nth(2).getByText('Delete').click()
await page.getByTestId('order').locator('css=dt:has-text("Total") + dd').innerText()

// Strictness: locators that match multiple elements FAIL, which is the point.
await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })).toHaveCount(1)   // explicit
// page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click()  ->  strict mode violation if 2 match
```

**Auto-waiting, and the two things that defeat it.**

```ts
// ✅ Auto-waits for clickability, visibility, stability (not animating), and enabled state.
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click()

// ✅ Auto-waits for the text to appear and to be stable.
await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 })

// ❌ Defeats auto-waiting: waiting for a state the app never sets.
await expect(page.locator('#app')).toHaveClass('loaded')      // implementation detail

// ❌ Defeats auto-waiting: a JS condition unrelated to the DOM.
await page.waitForFunction(() => (window as any).__ready === true)   // you have coupled to internals

// ❌ The forbidden one: an unconditional sleep.
await page.waitForTimeout(3000)     // always a defect, always a flake source
```

**Web-first assertions** are the reason Playwright tests are short and reliable:

```ts
await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders\/ord_/i)
await expect(page).toHaveTitle(/Checkout/)
await expect(locator).toBeVisible() / toBeHidden() / toBeEnabled() / toBeDisabled()
await expect(locator).toHaveText('£42.00')                  // full text (whitespace-normalised)
await expect(locator).toContainText('42.00')                // substring
await expect(locator).toHaveValue('ada@example.test')       // inputs
await expect(locator).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true')
await expect(locator).toHaveClass(/is-invalid/)
await expect(locator).toHaveCount(2)
await expect(locator).toBeChecked()                          // checkboxes/radios
await expect(locator).toHaveJSProperty('scrollWidth', 300)
await expect(locator).toBeInViewport()
await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png', { maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01 })
```

**Browser contexts: the isolation unit.** A `BrowserContext` is an incognito-like profile: its own cookies, `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB, permissions, geolocation, locale, timezone, and colour scheme. Creating one takes ~50ms versus ~1s for a new browser. This is what makes parallel tests cheap and isolated.

```ts
const context = await browser.newContext({
  locale: 'en-GB',
  timezoneId: 'Europe/London',
  colorScheme: 'dark',
  viewport: { width: 1280, height: 800 },
  storageState: await saveStorageState('admin'),   // reuse an authenticated profile
  permissions: ['clipboard-read', 'geolocation'],
  geolocation: { latitude: 51.5, longitude: -0.12 },
  extraHTTPHeaders: { 'X-Test-Run': process.env.RUN_ID },
  recordVideo: { dir: 'videos/', size: { width: 1280, height: 800 } },
  trace: 'retain-on-failure',
  screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
})
const page = await context.newPage()
```

**Fixtures: the mechanism for arrange and cleanup.**

```ts
// playwright/fixtures.ts
import { test as base, type Page } from '@playwright/test'

export type Fixtures = {
  api: ApiClient
  signIn: (email?: string, password?: string) => Promise<void>
  adminPage: Page
  seed: Seeder
}

export const test = base.extend<Fixtures>({
  // API client bound to this test's own namespace -- full isolation, parallel-safe.
  api: async ({}, use, testInfo) => {
    const ns = `${process.env.RUN_ID ?? 'local'}-${testInfo.workerIndex}-${testInfo.repeatEachIndex}-${testInfo.title.hashCode()}`
    const api = new ApiClient({ baseURL: process.env.API_URL!, namespace: ns, auth: { token: process.env.E2E_TOKEN! } })
    await use(api)
    await api.cleanupNamespace()      // runs even on failure: this is the isolation guarantee
  },

  signIn: async ({ page, api }, use) => {
    await use(async (email = 'ada@example.test', password = 'correct horse') => {
      await api.createUser({ email, password })
      const user = await api.login({ email, password })
      // Set the session the same way the app does, so the test uses the real auth path.
      await page.goto('/api/dev/session')                 // a test-only endpoint, gated by E2E_TOKEN
      await page.evaluate((token) => {
        ;(window as any).__e2eToken = token
      }, user.token)
      await page.goto('/')
    })
  },

  adminPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'test/.auth/admin.json' })
    const page = await context.newPage()
    await use(page)
    await context.close()
  },

  seed: async ({ api }, use) => { await use(new Seeder(api)) },
})

export { expect } from '@playwright/test'
```

**The config that makes a suite fast and useful.**

```ts
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test'

const isCI = !!process.env.CI

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  outputDir: './e2e/.artifacts',           // per-test artifacts (traces, videos, screenshots)
  fullyParallel: true,                    // tests in a file may run in parallel across workers
  forbidOnly: isCI,
  retries: isCI ? 1 : 0,                  // exactly 1; anything more is hiding flake
  workers: isCI ? process.env.CI_WORKERS ?? 4 : undefined,
  timeout: 45_000,                        // per test
  expect: { timeout: 7_500 },             // per assertion -- do not set this high
  globalTimeout: 20 * 60_000,             // the whole run; catches a hung test
  reporter: isCI
    ? [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['github'], ['junit', { outputFile: 'e2e/junit.xml' }], ['blob']]
    : [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['list']],

  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.E2E_BASE_URL ?? 'http://127.0.0.1:3100',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',           // the single most valuable setting
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure',
    actionTimeout: 10_000,
    navigationTimeout: 20_000,
    testIdAttribute: 'data-testid',
    ignoreHTTPSErrors: false,
    extraHTTPHeaders: isCI ? { 'X-Playwright-Run': process.env.RUN_ID ?? 'local' } : {},
  },

  expect: {
    toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01, animations: 'disabled', scale: 'css' },
  },

  // Projects = the browser x device matrix, and a stable set for visual baselines.
  projects: [
    { name: 'setup', testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/ },
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
    { name: 'firefox', use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] } },
    { name: 'webkit', use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] } },
    { name: 'mobile-chrome', use: { ...devices['Pixel 7'] } },
  ],

  webServer: [
    {
      command: 'pnpm build && pnpm start:preview',
      url: 'http://127.0.0.1:3100/healthz',
      reuseExistingServer: !isCI,
      timeout: 180_000,
      env: { NODE_ENV: 'test' },
    },
  ],
})
```

**Network control, which is the escape hatch you must have.**

```ts
// Block third-party noise so failures and timings are yours, not Facebook's.
await context.route('**/*', (route) => {
  const url = route.request().url()
  if (/google-analytics|doubleclick|hotjar|segment\.io/.test(url)) return route.abort()
  return route.continue()
})

// Stub a specific API to test a degraded state.
await page.route('**/api/recommendations', (route) =>
  route.fulfill({ status: 200, contentType: 'application/json', body: JSON.stringify({ items: [] }) }),
)

// Simulate a slow dependency precisely.
await page.route('**/api/slow', async (route) => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 8000)); await route.fulfill({ json: {} }) })

// Abort to simulate an offline failure of a specific call.
await page.route('**/api/payment-intent', (route) => route.fulfill({ status: 502, body: 'upstream down' }))

// NEVER route your own app's API in the happy path: it turns E2E into an integration test with extra steps.
```

**Tracing and debugging.**

```ts
test('checkout', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  // Explicit steps show in the trace's timeline, which makes triage fast.
  await test.step('add to basket', async () => { /* ... */ })
  await test.step('pay with card', async () => { /* ... */ })
  // Later, inspect:
  //   npx playwright show-trace e2e/.artifacts/checkout-abc123/trace.zip
})
```

```bash
# Replay a failed test with the trace, headed, no retries, and the trace viewer attached.
npx playwright test e2e/checkout.spec.ts --project=chromium --headed --retries=0 \
  --trace=on --reporter=list

# Re-run only the failed tests from the last run (blob reporter).
npx playwright merge-reports ./blob-report
npx playwright test --last-failed

# Codegen: record a session and generate a starting spec. The fastest way to bootstrap.
npx playwright codegen --save-storage=auth.json https://e2e.example.test

# Install only the browsers you need (a real CI time saver).
npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
```

**When to use Playwright vs not.**

Use it when: you need real-browser verification of journeys, you need all three engines, you want first-class tracing, you want fast parallel execution with cheap isolation, or you are starting a new E2E suite (its ergonomics and debugging are the best available).

Consider Cypress when: your team already knows it, or your testing is heavily component/DOM-oriented and you value its time-travel debugging. Consider Selenium (9.3.4) only for a legacy suite, an unusual device/grid requirement, or a WebDriver-only environment.

**Trade-offs.**

- **WebKit on Linux is not Safari.** It is close (same engine lineage) but not identical: font rendering, media codecs, and some platform APIs differ. Visual baselines must be generated per platform, and you should keep one real-Mac or BrowserStack job for Safari if Safari matters.
- **`fullyParallel: true` inside a file** is a step change for suite size, and it *forces* per-test data isolation. Teams that enable it must adopt API-based setup and namespaced cleanup; otherwise they trade slowness for flake.
- **Retry = 1 is a policy, not a setting.** A suite with 3% flake and `retries: 2` will be green and worthless. Track the flake rate (`flaky-tests` reporter) and treat it as a P1.
- **Auto-waiting hides real UX problems** in the sense that it waits for *stability*; a spinner that never resolves simply times out. That is a feature. But auto-waiting cannot wait for a condition your app never expresses in the DOM, so a test that needs `waitForFunction` is telling you the app lacks an observable state.
- **Trace files are large** (5-30MB). Budget artifact storage, upload on failure only, and set a retention policy.

**Production considerations.**

- `globalSetup`: apply migrations, seed reference data, and create an admin `storageState` file (`test/.auth/admin.json`) once per run rather than logging in per test.
- Pass a per-run namespace header (`X-Playwright-Run`) so DB cleanup can delete exactly this run's rows, and set a scheduled janitor to delete rows older than 24h.
- Use `test.info().project.name` in data ids so a test cannot collide across browser projects.
- On failure, upload `trace.zip`, `screenshot`, `video`, and the JUnit XML to CI artifacts with a 7-day retention.
- Set `workers` to the number of available cores, not more, and reduce it for video-enabled runs.
- Pin the Playwright version and the browser build together (`@playwright/test` 1.5x ships pinned browsers); upgrade the browsers on a schedule with visual-baseline regeneration in the same PR.

**Common mistakes.**

1. `page.waitForTimeout(3000)` everywhere -- the single largest source of flake and slowness in E2E suites.
2. `page.locator('.css-class')` or XPath instead of roles, so every markup refactor is a test migration.
3. A single `storageState` for all tests, so state leaks (a cart left in the basket) between tests.
4. Creating a new browser per test rather than a new context.
5. `retries: 3` as a flake remedy.
6. Relying on test execution order, with `fullyParallel` off and a `test.describe.serial`.
7. `page.route` stubbing your own API in the happy-path tests, which makes the E2E suite prove nothing.
8. Generating visual baselines on macOS but comparing in Linux containers -- every test fails on fonts.
9. No `trace: 'retain-on-failure'`, so triage is guesswork from the failure message.
10. Sharing a database with production-like data, so a test run can corrupt data other runs depend on.

**Interviewer probes.**

- 🟢 *"Explain Playwright's auto-waiting."* -- Locators are lazy and retry: each action polls until the element is visible, stable (not animating), enabled, and hit-testable; each assertion polls until it passes. So you write no explicit waits and still get deterministic behaviour.
- 🟡 *"Why create a new BrowserContext per test rather than a new browser?"* -- A context is an isolated incognito-like profile (cookies, storage, permissions, locale, timezone) that takes milliseconds, versus a second or more for a new browser process. That is what makes per-test isolation affordable.
- 🔴 *"Your E2E suite is 3% flaky. Walk me through the fix."* -- (1) Turn on tracing for every run and read ten traces; (2) classify: data, environment, timing, or product; (3) kill every `waitForTimeout` and replace with a locator assertion; (4) enable `fullyParallel` and per-test namespaced data; (5) check for shared state (storageState, DB, ports); (6) set `retries: 1` and start tracking the flake rate; (7) add a CI check that fails when quarantine grows.
- 🔴 *"When is a `BrowserContext` not enough isolation?"* -- When the resource lives outside the browser: a database, a Redis key, a file on disk, a queue, a third-party sandbox account. The context isolates cookies and storage only. That is why the API-level namespace in the fixture is mandatory.
- ⚫ *"WebKit vs Safari?"* -- WebKit is the same engine, but not the same browser: font rendering, media codecs, and some platform integrations differ, and it runs on Linux. Use WebKit for the majority of coverage and keep one real-Safari job (Mac runner or a cloud device farm) for the Safari-specific residue.

```ts
      await api.createUser({ email, password })
      const user = await api.login({ email, password })
      // Set the session the same way the app does, so the test uses the real auth path.
      await page.goto('/api/dev/session')                 // a test-only endpoint, gated by E2E_TOKEN
      await page.evaluate((token) => {
        ;(window as any).__e2eToken = token
      }, user.token)
      await page.goto('/')
    })
  },

  adminPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: 'test/.auth/admin.json' })
    const page = await context.newPage()
    await use(page)
    await context.close()
  },

  seed: async ({ api }, use) => { await use(new Seeder(api)) },

export { expect } from '@playwright/test'
```

**The config that makes a suite fast and useful.**

```ts
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test'

const isCI = !!process.env.CI

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  outputDir: './e2e/.artifacts',           // per-test artifacts (traces, videos, screenshots)
  fullyParallel: true,                    // tests in a file may run in parallel across workers
  forbidOnly: isCI,
  retries: isCI ? 1 : 0,                  // exactly 1; anything more is hiding flake
  workers: isCI ? process.env.CI_WORKERS ?? 4 : undefined,
  timeout: 45_000,                        // per test
  expect: { timeout: 7_500 },             // per assertion -- do not set this high
  globalTimeout: 20 * 60_000,             // the whole run; catches a hung test
  reporter: isCI
    ? [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['github'], ['junit', { outputFile: 'e2e/junit.xml' }], ['blob']]
    : [['html', { open: 'never' }], ['list']],

  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.E2E_BASE_URL ?? 'http://127.0.0.1:3100',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',           // the single most valuable setting
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure',
    actionTimeout: 10_000,
    navigationTimeout: 20_000,
    testIdAttribute: 'data-testid',
    ignoreHTTPSErrors: false,
    extraHTTPHeaders: isCI ? { 'X-Playwright-Run': process.env.RUN_ID ?? 'local' } : {},
  },

  expect: {
    toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01, animations: 'disabled', scale: 'css' },
  },

  // Projects = the browser x device matrix, and a stable set for visual baselines.
  projects: [
    { name: 'setup', testMatch: /global\.setup\.ts/ },
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
    { name: 'firefox', use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] } },
    { name: 'webkit', use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] } },
    { name: 'mobile-chrome', use: { ...devices['Pixel 7'] } },
  ],

  webServer: [
    {
      command: 'pnpm build && pnpm start:preview',
      url: 'http://127.0.0.1:3100/healthz',
      reuseExistingServer: !isCI,
      timeout: 180_000,
      env: { NODE_ENV: 'test' },
    },
  ],
})
```

**Network control, which is the escape hatch you must have.**

```ts
// Block third-party noise so failures and timings are yours, not Facebook's.
await context.route('**/*', (route) => {
  const url = route.request().url()
  if (/google-analytics|doubleclick|hotjar|segment\.io/.test(url)) return route.abort()
  return route.continue()
})

// Stub a specific API to test a degraded state.
await page.route('**/api/recommendations', (route) =>
  route.fulfill({ status: 200, contentType: 'application/json', body: JSON.stringify({ items: [] }) }),
)

// Simulate a slow dependency precisely.
await page.route('**/api/slow', async (route) => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 8000)); await route.fulfill({ json: {} }) })

// Abort to simulate an offline failure of a specific call.
await page.route('**/api/payment-intent', (route) => route.fulfill({ status: 502, body: 'upstream down' }))

// NEVER route your own app's API in the happy path: it turns E2E into an integration test with extra steps.
```

**Tracing and debugging.**

```ts
test('checkout', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  // Explicit steps show in the trace's timeline, which makes triage fast.
  await test.step('add to basket', async () => { /* ... */ })
  await test.step('pay with card', async () => { /* ... */ })
  // Later, inspect:
  //   npx playwright show-trace e2e/.artifacts/checkout-abc123/trace.zip
})
```

```bash
# Replay a failed test with the trace, headed, no retries, and the trace viewer attached.
npx playwright test e2e/checkout.spec.ts --project=chromium --headed --retries=0 \
  --trace=on --reporter=list

# Re-run only the failed tests from the last run (blob reporter).
npx playwright merge-reports ./blob-report
npx playwright test --last-failed

# Codegen: record a session and generate a starting spec. The fastest way to bootstrap.
npx playwright codegen --save-storage=auth.json https://e2e.example.test

# Install only the browsers you need (a real CI time saver).
npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
```

**When to use Playwright vs not.**

Use it when: you need real-browser verification of journeys, you need all three engines, you want first-class tracing, you want fast parallel execution with cheap isolation, or you are starting a new E2E suite (its ergonomics and debugging are the best available).

Consider Cypress when: your team already knows it, or your testing is heavily component/DOM-oriented and you value its time-travel debugging. Consider Selenium (9.3.4) only for a legacy suite, an unusual device/grid requirement, or a WebDriver-only environment.

**Trade-offs.**

- **WebKit on Linux is not Safari.** It is close (same engine lineage) but not identical: font rendering, media codecs, and some platform APIs differ. Visual baselines must be generated per platform, and you should keep one real-Mac or BrowserStack job for Safari if Safari matters.
- **`fullyParallel: true` inside a file** is a step change for suite size, and it *forces* per-test data isolation. Teams that enable it must adopt API-based setup and namespaced cleanup; otherwise they trade slowness for flake.
- **Retry = 1 is a policy, not a setting.** A suite with 3% flake and `retries: 2` will be green and worthless. Track the flake rate (`flaky-tests` reporter) and treat it as a P1.
- **Auto-waiting hides real UX problems** in the sense that it waits for *stability*; a spinner that never resolves simply times out. That is a feature. But auto-waiting cannot wait for a condition your app never expresses in the DOM, so a test that needs `waitForFunction` is telling you the app lacks an observable state.
- **Trace files are large** (5-30MB). Budget artifact storage, upload on failure only, and set a retention policy.

**Production considerations.**

- `globalSetup`: apply migrations, seed reference data, and create an admin `storageState` file (`test/.auth/admin.json`) once per run rather than logging in per test.
- Pass a per-run namespace header (`X-Playwright-Run`) so DB cleanup can delete exactly this run's rows, and set a scheduled janitor to delete rows older than 24h.
- Use `test.info().project.name` in data ids so a test cannot collide across browser projects.
- On failure, upload `trace.zip`, `screenshot`, `video`, and the JUnit XML to CI artifacts with a 7-day retention.
- Set `workers` to the number of available cores, not more, and reduce it for video-enabled runs.
- Pin the Playwright version and the browser build together (`@playwright/test` 1.5x ships pinned browsers); upgrade the browsers on a schedule with visual-baseline regeneration in the same PR.

**Common mistakes.**

1. `page.waitForTimeout(3000)` everywhere -- the single largest source of flake and slowness in E2E suites.
2. `page.locator('.css-class')` or XPath instead of roles, so every markup refactor is a test migration.
3. A single `storageState` for all tests, so state leaks (a cart left in the basket) between tests.
4. Creating a new browser per test rather than a new context.
5. `retries: 3` as a flake remedy.
6. Relying on test execution order, with `fullyParallel` off and a `test.describe.serial`.
7. `page.route` stubbing your own API in the happy-path tests, which makes the E2E suite prove nothing.
8. Generating visual baselines on macOS but comparing in Linux containers -- every test fails on fonts.
9. No `trace: 'retain-on-failure'`, so triage is guesswork from the failure message.
10. Sharing a database with production-like data, so a test run can corrupt data other runs depend on.

**Interviewer probes.**

- 🟢 *"Explain Playwright's auto-waiting."* -- Locators are lazy and retry: each action polls until the element is visible, stable (not animating), enabled, and hit-testable; each assertion polls until it passes. So you write no explicit waits and still get deterministic behaviour.
- 🟡 *"Why create a new BrowserContext per test rather than a new browser?"* -- A context is an isolated incognito-like profile (cookies, storage, permissions, locale, timezone) that takes milliseconds, versus a second or more for a new browser process. That is what makes per-test isolation affordable.
- 🔴 *"Your E2E suite is 3% flaky. Walk me through the fix."* -- (1) Turn on tracing for every run and read ten traces; (2) classify: data, environment, timing, or product; (3) kill every `waitForTimeout` and replace with a locator assertion; (4) enable `fullyParallel` and per-test namespaced data; (5) check for shared state (storageState, DB, ports); (6) set `retries: 1` and start tracking the flake rate; (7) add a CI check that fails when quarantine grows.
- 🔴 *"When is a `BrowserContext` not enough isolation?"* -- When the resource lives outside the browser: a database, a Redis key, a file on disk, a queue, a third-party sandbox account. The context isolates cookies and storage only. That is why the API-level namespace in the fixture is mandatory.
- ⚫ *"WebKit vs Safari?"* -- WebKit is the same engine, but not the same browser: font rendering, media codecs, and some platform integrations differ, and it runs on Linux. Use WebKit for the majority of coverage and keep one real-Safari job (Mac runner or a cloud device farm) for the Safari-specific residue.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition.**

**Cypress** (Cypress.io) is a browser-based end-to-end and component testing tool with a distinctive execution model. It runs *inside* the browser, in the same JS runtime as your application, which gives it two superpowers and one constraint.

**The superpowers.**
1. **Time travel.** Every test command is recorded with a snapshot of the DOM, the JavaScript state, network activity, and console output at that moment. When a test fails, you can hover backwards and inspect the application exactly as it was.
2. **Debuggability by construction.** `cy.pause()` opens a real debugger at that point in the test, and failures open the DevTools automatically.
3. **Deterministic command queue.** Commands are enqueued and executed in order, with retries on assertions (`should('be.visible')` retries for 4s by default), so you do not write waits.

**The constraint.** Because Cypress runs in the browser, it executes in the *same* page as your application. That means:
- It cannot run **multiple tabs** natively.
- It cannot visit **two superdomains in one test** (cross-origin navigation is restricted; `cy.visit` to a different origin is not supported in the same test).
- It is **not a real WebDriver**, so testing native browser features (the file picker, some OS dialogs, WebAuthn, real downloads in some modes) is harder.
- It requires a **proxy** in front of your app, which is a real deployment-shape difference (and occasionally a real source of CORS/cookie bugs that do not exist in production).

**Mechanics -- the vocabulary, which is the main learning curve.**

```ts
// Cypress
describe('checkout', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    cy.intercept('POST', '/api/orders').as('createOrder')     // "intercept" + "alias"
    cy.visit('/shop')
  })

  it('completes a purchase', () => {
    cy.get('[data-cy=add-to-basket]').click()                  // data-cy is the Cypress convention
    cy.contains('button', 'Checkout').click()                 // contains() = text + selector
    cy.get('#card').type('4242424242424242')                  // .type() is the user-like input
    cy.get('[data-cy=submit]').click()

    cy.wait('@createOrder').its('response.statusCode').should('eq', 201)   // alias wait
    cy.contains('Thank you for your order').should('be.visible')           // auto-retrying
  })

  it('fails fast on an API error', () => {
    cy.intercept('POST', '/api/orders', { statusCode: 500, body: { error: 'boom' } })
    cy.get('[data-cy=submit]').click()
    cy.contains("We couldn't complete your order").should('be.visible')
  })
})
```

**Where Cypress differs from Playwright, concretely.**

| Dimension | Cypress | Playwright |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Execution | in-browser, in the app's page/context | out-of-process, via CDP/Juggler/WebDriver-class protocols |
| Commands | queued, imperative chain | async/await, promise-like |
| Retrying assertions | `should()` retries by default | `expect().toX()` retries by default |
| Multi-tab | not supported | native |
| Cross-origin in one test | not supported | supported |
| iframes | `cy.iframe()` plugin-ish; `cy.origin()` for cross-origin | first-class `frameLocator()` |
| Shadow DOM | limited | first-class piercing locators |
| Component testing | **first-class and a major strength** | available via Vitest Browser Mode / CT |
| Parallelism | paid Cloud feature (free split via sharding is limited) | free, first-class, any CI |
| Trace viewer | time travel + DevTools, no separate trace artefact | `trace.zip` viewer |
| Browser support | Chromium-family, Firefox, Edge, WebKit (Electron-based runner) | Chromium, Firefox, WebKit |
| Best fit | component/DOM-heavy testing, single-tab journeys, rich debugging | multi-browser, multi-tab, parallel, E2E at scale |
| Bundle cost | large, must be in the dev build only | separate package, not shipped |

**Code that shows the model difference most clearly: waiting for something that is not an element.**

```ts
// Cypress: retrying assertion on a non-DOM value, via `should(callback)`
cy.get('[data-cy=spin]').should('not.exist')
cy.wrap(sessionStore.get('cartId')).should('equal', 123)   // no DOM required
cy.get('[data-cy=item]').should(($els) => {
  expect($els).to.have.length(3)                            // custom retryable assertion
})

// Playwright: same idea
await expect(page.locator('[data-cy=item]')).toHaveCount(3)
await expect.poll(() => sessionStore.get('cartId')).toBe(123)   // expect.poll for non-DOM state
```

**Mechanics -- `cy.intercept`, which is Cypress's MSW and its most useful feature.**

```ts
// Static stub
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/user', { statusCode: 200, body: { id: 'usr_1', name: 'Ada' } })

// Dynamic stub with a request handler
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/orders/*', (req) => {
  req.reply((res) => {
    res.send({ ...res.body, lines: [] })
  })
})

// Delay, for loading-state tests
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/slow', (req) => {
  req.on('response', (res) => res.setDelay(3000))     // delay the response
  req.continue()
})

// Fail the request entirely (network error)
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/fragile', { forceNetworkError: true })

// Alias for waiting and asserting
cy.intercept('POST', '/api/orders').as('createOrder')
cy.wait('@createOrder').its('request.body').should('deep.equal', expected)

// Add a header to every request
cy.intercept({ url: '**/api/**' }, (req) => { req.headers['x-e2e'] = '1'; req.continue() })
```

**Component testing in Cypress is its real differentiator.**

```tsx
// cypress/component/OrderSummary.cy.tsx -- mounts a component with real providers
import { mount } from 'cypress/react18'
import { MemoryRouter } from 'react-router-dom'

describe('<OrderSummary />', () => {
  it('renders the total', () => {
    mount(
      <MemoryRouter>
        <OrderSummary orderId="ord_1" />
      </MemoryRouter>,
    )
    cy.contains('Total: £42.00').should('be.visible')
  })

  it('shows an error state', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/orders/ord_1', { statusCode: 503, body: {} })
    mount(<MemoryRouter><OrderSummary orderId="ord_1" /></MemoryRouter>)
    cy.contains('We could not load this order').should('be.visible')
  })
})
```

```ts
// cypress.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress'
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:3100',
    specPattern: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts',
    supportFile: 'cypress/support/e2e.ts',
    viewportWidth: 1280,
    viewportHeight: 800,
    defaultCommandTimeout: 8000,
    retries: { runMode: 1, openMode: 0 },
    video: false,
    screenshotOnRunFailure: true,
    setupNodeEvents(on) {
      on('before:browser:launch', (browser, launchOptions) => {
        if (browser.family === 'chromium') launchOptions.args.push('--disable-dev-shm-usage')
        return launchOptions
      })
    },
  },
  component: {
    devServer: { framework: 'react', bundler: 'vite' },
    specPattern: 'cypress/component/**/*.cy.tsx',
    supportFile: 'cypress/support/component.tsx',
  },
})
```

**When to use Cypress vs Playwright.**

Cypress when: your team knows it, your testing is heavily component/DOM-oriented (its component testing with real providers and `cy.intercept` is excellent), your journeys are single-tab, and the debugging affordances are worth more to your team than multi-tab support and free parallelism.

Playwright when: you need multi-tab, cross-origin flows, real parallel execution at scale, or you are starting fresh and want the more capable default.

**Trade-offs.**

- **Cypress's in-browser model is a genuine architectural constraint**, not a preference: multi-tab, cross-origin, and some native browser features are simply out of reach. Migrating later is expensive.
- **Parallelism cost.** Free, first-class parallelism is Playwright's structural advantage. If you are on Cypress and need it, the honest options are Cypress Cloud (paid) or splitting specs across CI jobs (workable, more config).
- **Cypress bundles a browser and a large runtime into your app's dev build.** It is never shipped to production, but it does affect your dev bundle and must be conditionally imported.
- **Time travel is uniquely good for UI failures** and has no Playwright equivalent -- though Playwright's trace covers much of the same ground in a form that works in CI.
- **`cy.then()` and queue semantics** trip up people coming from Playwright, and mixing promises into the chain causes "returned a promise from a command" errors.

**Common mistakes.**

1. `cy.wait(1000)` -- Cypress's `cy.wait` with a number is discouraged in favour of alias waits; it is the same anti-pattern as `waitForTimeout`.
2. Using `data-cy` everywhere instead of accessible queries, which locks you to the test attribute.
3. `cy.get()` on an element inside an iframe without `cy.origin()` for cross-origin iframes.
4. Testing multi-tab behaviour and discovering Cypress cannot do it, after committing to it.
5. Adding a fixed `baseUrl` that differs from production's path prefix, so routing tests pass and production fails.
6. `cy.intercept` stubbing your own API in every test, making the suite prove only that your React app renders.

**Interviewer probes.**

- 🟢 *"What is Cypress's distinctive execution model, and what does it buy you?"* -- It runs inside the browser, in the same context as the app, which gives time travel (DOM/JS/network snapshots at every step) and first-class debugging, plus deterministic command queuing with auto-retrying assertions. The cost is no multi-tab, no cross-origin navigation in one test, and a proxy-based dev topology.
- 🟡 *"When would you choose Cypress over Playwright?"* -- When component/DOM testing is a large part of your suite and you value the debugging affordances, your journeys are single-tab, and the team is already productive in it. Not when you need multi-tab, heavy parallelism, or cross-origin flows.
- 🔴 *"How do you test a multi-tab flow in Cypress, given its model?"* -- You cannot, natively. Options: (1) drive the second tab with direct Playwright/CDP from a separate process and coordinate through the API; (2) refactor the feature so cross-tab communication is mediated by the server or `BroadcastChannel` and test the *contract* rather than the second tab; (3) choose Playwright. Asserting on `localStorage` `storage` events is a proxy, not a real test.
- 🔴 *"`cy.wait(2000)` vs `cy.wait('@alias')`?"* -- The numeric wait is a fixed sleep that is slow when unnecessary and flaky when insufficient. Alias waits block until the named request completes, then let you assert on its request and response, which is both faster and a real assertion.
- ⚫ *"What is `cy.origin` for?"* -- Cypress's escape hatch for interacting with a cross-origin iframe: you must re-declare your commands inside the callback because Cypress cannot inject its script into another origin. It works, but it is a signal that the architecture crosses origins in a way that deserves a second look.

```ts
cy.intercept('GET', '/api/fragile', { forceNetworkError: true })

// Alias for waiting and asserting
cy.intercept('POST', '/api/orders').as('createOrder')
cy.wait('@createOrder').its('request.body').should('deep.equal', expected)

// Add a header to every request
cy.intercept({ url: '**/api/**' }, (req) => { req.headers['x-e2e'] = '1'; req.continue() })
```

**Component testing in Cypress is its real differentiator.**

```tsx
// cypress/component/OrderSummary.cy.tsx -- mounts a component with real providers
import { mount } from 'cypress/react18'
import { MemoryRouter } from 'react-router-dom'

describe('<OrderSummary />', () => {
  it('renders the total', () => {
    mount(
      <MemoryRouter>
        <OrderSummary orderId="ord_1" />
      </MemoryRouter>,
    )
    cy.contains('Total: £42.00').should('be.visible')
  })

  it('shows an error state', () => {
    cy.intercept('GET', '/api/orders/ord_1', { statusCode: 503, body: {} })
    mount(<MemoryRouter><OrderSummary orderId="ord_1" /></MemoryRouter>)
    cy.contains('We could not load this order').should('be.visible')
  })
})
```

```ts
import { defineConfig } from 'cypress'
export default defineConfig({
  e2e: {
    baseUrl: 'http://127.0.0.1:3100',
    specPattern: 'cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts',
    supportFile: 'cypress/support/e2e.ts',
    viewportWidth: 1280,
    viewportHeight: 800,
    defaultCommandTimeout: 8000,
    retries: { runMode: 1, openMode: 0 },
    video: false,
    screenshotOnRunFailure: true,
    setupNodeEvents(on) {
      on('before:browser:launch', (browser, launchOptions) => {
        if (browser.family === 'chromium') launchOptions.args.push('--disable-dev-shm-usage')
        return launchOptions
      })
    },
  },
  component: {
```

**When to use Cypress vs Playwright.**

Cypress when: your team knows it, your testing is heavily component/DOM-oriented (its component testing with real providers and `cy.intercept` is excellent), your journeys are single-tab, and the debugging affordances are worth more to your team than multi-tab support and free parallelism.

Playwright when: you need multi-tab, cross-origin flows, real parallel execution at scale, or you are starting fresh and want the more capable default.

**Trade-offs.**

- **Cypress's in-browser model is a genuine architectural constraint**, not a preference: multi-tab, cross-origin, and some native browser features are simply out of reach. Migrating later is expensive.
- **Parallelism cost.** Free, first-class parallelism is Playwright's structural advantage. If you are on Cypress and need it, the honest options are Cypress Cloud (paid) or splitting specs across CI jobs (workable, more config).
- **Cypress bundles a browser and a large runtime into your app's dev build.** It is never shipped to production, but it does affect your dev bundle and must be conditionally imported.
- **Time travel is uniquely good for UI failures** and has no Playwright equivalent -- though Playwright's trace covers much of the same ground in a form that works in CI.
- **`cy.then()` and queue semantics** trip up people coming from Playwright, and mixing promises into the chain causes "returned a promise from a command" errors.

**Common mistakes.**

1. `cy.wait(1000)` -- Cypress's `cy.wait` with a number is discouraged in favour of alias waits; it is the same anti-pattern as `waitForTimeout`.
2. Using `data-cy` everywhere instead of accessible queries, which locks you to the test attribute.
3. `cy.get()` on an element inside an iframe without `cy.origin()` for cross-origin iframes.
4. Testing multi-tab behaviour and discovering Cypress cannot do it, after committing to it.
5. Adding a fixed `baseUrl` that differs from production's path prefix, so routing tests pass and production fails.
6. `cy.intercept` stubbing your own API in every test, making the suite prove only that your React app renders.

**Interviewer probes.**

- 🟢 *"What is Cypress's distinctive execution model, and what does it buy you?"* -- It runs inside the browser, in the same context as the app, which gives time travel (DOM/JS/network snapshots at every step) and first-class debugging, plus deterministic command queuing with auto-retrying assertions. The cost is no multi-tab, no cross-origin navigation in one test, and a proxy-based dev topology.
- 🟡 *"When would you choose Cypress over Playwright?"* -- When component/DOM testing is a large part of your suite and you value the debugging affordances, your journeys are single-tab, and the team is already productive in it. Not when you need multi-tab, heavy parallelism, or cross-origin flows.
- 🔴 *"How do you test a multi-tab flow in Cypress, given its model?"* -- You cannot, natively. Options: (1) drive the second tab with direct Playwright/CDP from a separate process and coordinate through the API; (2) refactor the feature so cross-tab communication is mediated by the server or `BroadcastChannel` and test the *contract* rather than the second tab; (3) choose Playwright. Asserting on `localStorage` `storage` events is a proxy, not a real test.
- 🔴 *"`cy.wait(2000)` vs `cy.wait('@alias')`?"* -- The numeric wait is a fixed sleep that is slow when unnecessary and flaky when insufficient. Alias waits block until the named request completes, then let you assert on its request and response, which is both faster and a real assertion.
- ⚫ *"What is `cy.origin` for?"* -- Cypress's escape hatch for interacting with a cross-origin iframe: you must re-declare your commands inside the callback because Cypress cannot inject its script into another origin. It works, but it is a signal that the architecture crosses origins in a way that deserves a second look.

topics.title: Selenium and the WebDriver protocol, for awareness
topics.description: Selenium and the WebDriver protocol, for awareness within End-to-End Testing.
keyConcepts: Selenium
Why you still need to know it (2026)
It is the only option for some environments: real Safari on real macOS via safaridriver (managed by Apple), legacy devices, and some enterprise grids.
It is the substrate of Appium, which drives native and hybrid mobile apps with the same WebDriver model. Any mobile native-testing strategy you meet will use it.
It is the interop reference for any automation tool: WebDriver is the standard the other tools are measured against.
Many organisations have an existing Selenium suite or grid, and migrating is a project, not a decision.
Understanding the protocol makes you understand what the modern tools abstract away (the session, the element lookup, the shadow root, the action sequence, the document readiness).
The four hard parts of Selenium, and how the modern tools solve them

Waiting. WebDriver is unopinionated: an element may be located but not yet clickable, and click() throws ElementNotInteractableException. The answer is driver.wait(until.elementIsVisible(...)) or explicit ExpectedConditions. Every Selenium suite is 30% waiting code. Playwright and Cypress build retrying locators into the API, so this code does not exist.

Driver/browsers version matching. Historically the biggest tax in Selenium. Selenium Manager (4.6+) bundles a binary that resolves and caches the right driver for the installed browser. This single change removed a whole category of support tickets.

Grid and distribution. Selenium Grid 4 provides a hub and node architecture, W3C-compliant, with Docker/Kubernetes deployment and session routing policies (strict, dynamic, fixed). It is still the answer for "we must run on 40 real devices/OS versions in one place".
No first-class tracing. You build artifact capture yourself (screenshots, getPageSource, network logs via BiDi). Modern tools do this for you.

topics.title: Page object model: when it helps and when it hides the test
topics.description: Page object model: when it helps and when it hides the test within End-to-End Testing.
keyConcepts: The POM that hides the test -- the failure mode, named
The page object returns data and the test asserts everything. Then the page object is a "getter bag" and the assertions are in the test; you have the worst of both.
The page object contains business logic. await cart.applyCouponIfOrderOver(50) now duplicates a pricing rule that a unit test owns, and it will drift.
The page object hides failures. A method that internally retries, catches, and falls back will make a broken app look like a passing test.
The page object is a one-line wrapper. get addButton() { return this.page.locator('#add') } adds indirection and no value.

Selectors are stored as fields at construction time. private readonly qty = page.locator('#qty') binds the locator before navigation; in Playwright a locator is lazy so this is usually fine, but with page.$ (a promise) it captures the wrong element. Always store the Page, not resolved elements.

One page object per screen means N objects per test. The combinatorial cost is what pushes teams to abandon the pattern -- and then the selectors leak back into the tests, and every copy change breaks 40 tests.
The decision rule, and what to do instead
POM pros: one place to change when the UI changes; readable tests; reusable flows; a natural home for waits and for i18n; keeps test files focused on intent.

POM cons: indirection makes failures harder to localise (a stack trace points into the page object, not the test); over-abstraction makes tests read like a DSL nobody but the author can use; and a page object per screen multiplies the files you must maintain.

Capability objects beat page objects on intent-readability and navigation-resilience, at the cost of being less "reusable" for flows that only one test uses. Given that E2E suites should be small and intent-focused, this is the right trade.

Never put assertions in a page object that are about the *test's* data (e.g. "this order is in the database"); keep those in the test. Assertions about the *screen's* state belong with the screen's capability.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition.**

**Visual regression testing** (also called screenshot testing, VRT, or screenshot diffing) captures a rendered screenshot of a UI in a known state and compares it, pixel by pixel, against a committed baseline. It is the only automated way to catch a class of regression that no functional test can see: a broken layout, a misaligned baseline, a missing font, a clipped text, a wrong colour, a broken responsive breakpoint, an icon that fails to load, a dark-mode regression, or a hydration mismatch that leaves the page half-styled.

**Mechanics -- the four problems, and the solutions that work.**

1. **Nondeterminism.** Animations, transitions, carousels, clocks, random data, cursor position, and scrollbars produce different pixels on every run.
2. **Font rendering differences** between OSes and even between machines with different font versions.
3. **Sub-pixel and anti-aliasing noise** from fractional layout.
4. **Dynamic content** (dates, names, "3 minutes ago", randomised ids).

Solutions, in order of importance:

```ts
// 1. Freeze time, seed randomness, and disable animation in the *app* for tests.
await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-03-01T09:00:00Z') })     // Playwright 1.45+
await page.addInitScript(() => {
  // Deterministic randomness
  let seed = 42
  Math.random = () => { seed = (seed * 1664525 + 1013904223) >>> 0; return seed / 2 ** 32 }
  // No transitions/animations
  const style = document.createElement('style')
  style.textContent = `*, *::before, *::after { animation: none !important; transition: none !important;
                    caret-color: transparent !important; scroll-behavior: auto !important; }`
  document.head.appendChild(style)
})
// Web fonts: wait for them, so you never screenshot a fallback font.
await page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready)

// 2. The config: masks, tolerances, and a stable rendering environment.
expect: {
  toHaveScreenshot: {
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,      // 1% of pixels may differ; raise for text-heavy pages
    threshold: 0.2,               // per-pixel colour tolerance 0-1
    animations: 'disabled',       // wait for CSS animations to finish
    caret: 'hide',                // hide the text cursor
    scale: 'css',                 // screenshot in CSS pixels, not device pixels
    stylePath: path.join(__dirname, 'visual.css'),   // per-test CSS overrides
  },
}

// 3. Mask the parts that can never be stable.
await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png', {
  mask: [page.getByTestId('order-id'), page.getByTestId('relative-time')],
  maskColor: '#FF00FF',          // a colour that never appears in the design system
  fullPage: true,
})
```

**Where visual baselines live, and how they are reviewed.** Baselines are binary PNGs in git. This creates a real workflow problem, and the honest workflow is:

```bash
# Locally: run the visual tests, get diffs, inspect them in the HTML report
npx playwright test --update-snapshots      # regenerate
npx playwright show-report                  # open the report with side-by-side diffs

# In PR: a human must look at the diff images. The report is a CI artefact.
```

Practical rules that keep this workable:
- **Keep the baseline count low.** 20-40 screenshots per platform for critical screens; not every page. Visual coverage of stable, high-value screens only.
- **Group shots into few files.** One screenshot per "state" (empty, loading, error, populated, mobile, desktop) rather than one per component.
- **Freeze a platform for baselines.** Generate them in the same container image you compare in, so fonts and rendering are identical. In CI, use the official Playwright Docker image.
- **Threshold is not a licence.** A 5% diff ratio on a text-heavy page will accept a completely different paragraph. Prefer masking text to loosening thresholds.

**Playwright's visual comparison is the practical default.**

```ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'

// A single, table-driven visual spec keeps the baseline count and the maintenance cost low.
const STATES = [
  { name: 'empty', setup: async (page: Page) => { await api.setCart([]) } },
  { name: 'single-item', setup: async (page: Page) => { await api.setCart([{ sku: 'WIDGET', qty: 1 }]) } },
  { name: 'many-items', setup: async (page: Page) => { await api.setCart(bulkCart(40)) } },
  { name: 'price-error', setup: async (page: Page) => { await api.setPriceError('SKU', 'unavailable') } },
]

for (const state of STATES) {
  test(`basket -- ${state.name}`, async ({ page, api }) => {
    await api.setViewportProfile('member')
    await state.setup(page)
    await page.goto('/basket')
    await expect(page.getByRole('region', { name: 'Basket' })).toBeVisible()
    await expect(page.getByTestId('basket-settled')).toBeAttached()   // explicit app-level "ready" signal
    await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(`basket-${state.name}.png`, { fullPage: true })
  })
}

test('basket -- dark mode', async ({ page, api }) => {
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark', reducedMotion: 'reduce' })
  await api.setCart([{ sku: 'WIDGET', qty: 1 }])
  await page.goto('/basket')
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('basket-dark.png')
})

test('basket -- long content does not break layout', async ({ page, api }) => {
  await api.setCart([{ sku: 'A-VERY-LONG-SKU-THAT-SHOULD-NOT-OVERFLOW-OR-WRAP-THE-LAYOUT', qty: 999_999 }])
  await page.goto('/basket')
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('basket-long-content.png')
})
```

**The explicit ready signal is important and often missing.** `toHaveScreenshot` waits for fonts and two animation frames, but your data may still be loading. Add a `data-settled` attribute set by the app when the view is in its final state:

```tsx
// In the app, under a test-friendly flag.
export function BasketView({ state }: { state: BasketState }) {
  return (
    <section
      aria-label="Basket"
      data-testid="basket-settled"
      data-settled={state.status === 'ready'}
      hidden={state.status !== 'ready'}
    >
      {/* ... */}
    </section>
  )
}
// Then: await expect(page.getByTestId('basket-settled')).toHaveAttribute('data-settled', 'true')
```

**Other visual regression tools, briefly, for awareness.**

- **Percy** (BrowserStack): hosted, cross-browser baselines, good review workflow, paid.
- **Chromatic** (Storybook): component-level visual testing, excellent for design systems, integrates with Storybook, paid with a free tier.
- **BackstopJS** / **Loki**: config-as-code, Docker, self-hosted, good for teams that want their own pipeline.
- **Argos / Happo**: similar hosted options.
- **jest-image-snapshot / @vitest/image-snapshot**: component-level image comparison inside your unit/component suite -- useful for canvas and chart output, not for full pages.

**When to use visual regression vs not.**

Use it for: layout and responsive-breakpoint regressions, design system components, dark/high-contrast/print modes, error and empty states that must look specific, and any screen where a visual change is a product change (marketing pages, onboarding, checkout).

Do not use it for: verifying that a button works (functional test), for every page of a large app (the maintenance and review cost explodes), or for screens whose content is inherently user-specific with no masking possible (a dashboard of arbitrary customer data -- use masked component shots instead).

**Trade-offs.**

- **It catches what nothing else can.** A one-pixel misalignment, a font that failed to load, a flex container that collapsed on a 320px viewport, a z-index regression hiding a button. No functional test sees these.
- **It is noisy, and noise is fatal.** A suite where 5% of runs differ without a change gets ignored, and then it catches nothing. The discipline is: freeze time, freeze randomness, mask dynamic regions, pin the rendering environment, and keep the count low.
- **Baseline review is a human process.** A PR with 15 changed screenshots requires a designer or a careful engineer to look at each one. Automating the review is not possible; automating the *generation* is.
- **Font licensing and availability** are a real operational problem. If the app uses a licensed webfont, your CI container needs it, and your dev machines need it, or every baseline is wrong.
- **It does not tell you *why*.** A diff image shows that something changed; finding the cause is still manual.
- **Platform-specific baselines multiply the work.** Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit baselines are three sets. Generate all three but review them as one logical group, and accept that only the Chromium set needs to be pristine.

**Common mistakes.**

1. Animations and carousels not frozen, so every run differs.
2. Screenshots taken before data has loaded, so the baseline is a spinner.
3. Unstable content (relative times, order ids, avatars from a CDN) not masked, so the suite is 100% flake.
4. Baselines generated on a developer Mac and compared in a Linux container -- font rendering guarantees failure.
5. A `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.2` "fix" that accepts any layout change.
6. Snapshotting full pages of dynamic dashboards, so the baseline is meaningless.
7. Auto-updating baselines in CI, which silently accepts every visual regression.
8. Reviewing the diff images not at all, so visual tests exist but protect nothing.
9. Testing only the default viewport; the regressions happen at 320px and at 1920px.

**Interviewer probes.**

- 🟢 *"What is visual regression testing and what does it catch that functional tests cannot?"* -- Comparing a rendered screenshot against a committed baseline, which catches layout, styling, font-loading, breakpoint, colour, and z-index regressions that no DOM assertion can see.
- 🟡 *"How do you stop a visual suite being flaky?"* -- Freeze the clock, seed randomness, disable animations and transitions, wait for web fonts, wait for an explicit app-level "settled" signal, mask every dynamic region, generate and compare baselines in the same pinned container image, and use a per-pixel threshold rather than a large ratio.
- 🔴 *"Your visual suite is 20% flaky. Diagnose."* -- Look at the failing diffs and classify: animation (not frozen), timing (screenshot before settled), data (unmasked dynamic content), environment (fonts or GPU), or genuine nondeterminism (a random layout-affecting value). In that order; animation and timing account for most cases.
- 🔴 *"Should a designer be in the visual review loop?"* -- Yes, for the same reason a designer is in the design review loop: visual changes are product changes, and the diff image is the cheapest possible design review artefact. If there is no designer available, at minimum require an explicit human approval step on any PR with changed baselines, so a regression cannot be merged by accident.
- ⚫ *"How do you test a page with a live chat widget and a rotating ad?"* -- Mask both regions in the assertion (`mask: [chatWidget, adSlot]`), stub the ad and chat requests at the network layer so they render a fixed placeholder, and disable their animations. If a region cannot be both stubbed and masked (e.g. it is above the fold and its absence changes layout), exclude that state from visual testing and cover it functionally.

---

```ts
  await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark', reducedMotion: 'reduce' })
  await api.setCart([{ sku: 'WIDGET', qty: 1 }])
  await page.goto('/basket')
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('basket-dark.png')
})

test('basket -- long content does not break layout', async ({ page, api }) => {
  await api.setCart([{ sku: 'A-VERY-LONG-SKU-THAT-SHOULD-NOT-OVERFLOW-OR-WRAP-THE-LAYOUT', qty: 999_999 }])
  await page.goto('/basket')
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('basket-long-content.png')
})
```

**The explicit ready signal is important and often missing.** `toHaveScreenshot` waits for fonts and two animation frames, but your data may still be loading. Add a `data-settled` attribute set by the app when the view is in its final state:

```tsx
// In the app, under a test-friendly flag.
export function BasketView({ state }: { state: BasketState }) {
  return (
    <section
      aria-label="Basket"
      data-testid="basket-settled"
      data-settled={state.status === 'ready'}
      hidden={state.status !== 'ready'}
    >
      {/* ... */}
    </section>
  )
}
// Then: await expect(page.getByTestId('basket-settled')).toHaveAttribute('data-settled', 'true')
```

**Other visual regression tools, briefly, for awareness.**

- **Percy** (BrowserStack): hosted, cross-browser baselines, good review workflow, paid.
- **Chromatic** (Storybook): component-level visual testing, excellent for design systems, integrates with Storybook, paid with a free tier.
- **BackstopJS** / **Loki**: config-as-code, Docker, self-hosted, good for teams that want their own pipeline.
- **Argos / Happo**: similar hosted options.
- **jest-image-snapshot / @vitest/image-snapshot**: component-level image comparison inside your unit/component suite -- useful for canvas and chart output, not for full pages.

**When to use visual regression vs not.**

Use it for: layout and responsive-breakpoint regressions, design system components, dark/high-contrast/print modes, error and empty states that must look specific, and any screen where a visual change is a product change (marketing pages, onboarding, checkout).

Do not use it for: verifying that a button works (functional test), for every page of a large app (the maintenance and review cost explodes), or for screens whose content is inherently user-specific with no masking possible (a dashboard of arbitrary customer data -- use masked component shots instead).

**Trade-offs.**

- **It catches what nothing else can.** A one-pixel misalignment, a font that failed to load, a flex container that collapsed on a 320px viewport, a z-index regression hiding a button. No functional test sees these.
- **It is noisy, and noise is fatal.** A suite where 5% of runs differ without a change gets ignored, and then it catches nothing. The discipline is: freeze time, freeze randomness, mask dynamic regions, pin the rendering environment, and keep the count low.
- **Baseline review is a human process.** A PR with 15 changed screenshots requires a designer or a careful engineer to look at each one. Automating the review is not possible; automating the *generation* is.
- **Font licensing and availability** are a real operational problem. If the app uses a licensed webfont, your CI container needs it, and your dev machines need it, or every baseline is wrong.
- **It does not tell you *why*.** A diff image shows that something changed; finding the cause is still manual.
- **Platform-specific baselines multiply the work.** Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit baselines are three sets. Generate all three but review them as one logical group, and accept that only the Chromium set needs to be pristine.

**Common mistakes.**

1. Animations and carousels not frozen, so every run differs.
2. Screenshots taken before data has loaded, so the baseline is a spinner.
3. Unstable content (relative times, order ids, avatars from a CDN) not masked, so the suite is 100% flake.
4. Baselines generated on a developer Mac and compared in a Linux container -- font rendering guarantees failure.
5. A `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.2` "fix" that accepts any layout change.
6. Snapshotting full pages of dynamic dashboards, so the baseline is meaningless.
7. Auto-updating baselines in CI, which silently accepts every visual regression.
8. Reviewing the diff images not at all, so visual tests exist but protect nothing.
9. Testing only the default viewport; the regressions happen at 320px and at 1920px.

**Interviewer probes.**

- 🟢 *"What is visual regression testing and what does it catch that functional tests cannot?"* -- Comparing a rendered screenshot against a committed baseline, which catches layout, styling, font-loading, breakpoint, colour, and z-index regressions that no DOM assertion can see.
- 🟡 *"How do you stop a visual suite being flaky?"* -- Freeze the clock, seed randomness, disable animations and transitions, wait for web fonts, wait for an explicit app-level "settled" signal, mask every dynamic region, generate and compare baselines in the same pinned container image, and use a per-pixel threshold rather than a large ratio.
- 🔴 *"Your visual suite is 20% flaky. Diagnose."* -- Look at the failing diffs and classify: animation (not frozen), timing (screenshot before settled), data (unmasked dynamic content), environment (fonts or GPU), or genuine nondeterminism (a random layout-affecting value). In that order; animation and timing account for most cases.
- 🔴 *"Should a designer be in the visual review loop?"* -- Yes, for the same reason a designer is in the design review loop: visual changes are product changes, and the diff image is the cheapest possible design review artefact. If there is no designer available, at minimum require an explicit human approval step on any PR with changed baselines, so a regression cannot be merged by accident.
- ⚫ *"How do you test a page with a live chat widget and a rotating ad?"* -- Mask both regions in the assertion (`mask: [chatWidget, adSlot]`), stub the ad and chat requests at the network layer so they render a fixed placeholder, and disable their animations. If a region cannot be both stubbed and masked (e.g. it is above the fold and its absence changes layout), exclude that state from visual testing and cover it functionally.

---

topics.title: Network conditions, throttling, and offline
topics.description: Network conditions, throttling, and offline within End-to-End Testing.
keyConcepts: Network condition testing
The behaviours worth testing (the canonical list)
When to test network conditions

Throttling makes tests slow -- a 3G test can take 30s. Keep it to one or two tests per critical journey, and use page.route delays (portable) rather than CDP throughput emulation (accurate but Chromium-only and slower).

CDP network emulation is Chromium-only, so a throttling test in the WebKit/Firefox projects will silently do nothing if you write it with newCDPSession. Guard it with test.skip(browserName !== 'chromium') or use route-based delays.

Service workers complicate everything. A service worker may serve a cached response and never hit the network, so your throttle test measures nothing. Test service-worker behaviour explicitly (a dedicated context with serviceWorkers: 'block', and another with them enabled).
Realistic offline testing requires a real offline story. If the app has no offline capability, "offline" is just "an error page", and that is a product finding, not a test.
Randomised fault injection produces flaky tests. Make faults deterministic (specific paths, specific counts, specific order) so a failure is reproducible.
setOffline on the context but the app uses a service worker that serves from cache, so nothing changes.
Testing throttling in the WebKit project with a CDP-only call.
Asserting a fixed time (expect(elapsed).toBeGreaterThan(3000)), which is a load test not an E2E test.
Not testing the *reconnect* path, which is where duplicate writes and data loss live.

topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition.**

**CI integration** for testing means the pipeline design that decides which tests run when, on what, in what order, with what parallelism, and what blocks a merge. **Sharding** is splitting the test set into N roughly equal-duration groups that run in parallel, so wall-clock time falls as 1/N. Both are quality mechanisms: a test that does not run on every change is not a test.

**Mechanics -- the pipeline shape that works, and why each stage exists.**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true                 # never waste CI on a superseded commit

jobs:
  # ── Stage 1: the fast gate. 20 seconds, hard required. Nobody waits for this.
  verify:
    name: Lint, types, unit, property
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint
      - run: pnpm typecheck                     # tsc --noEmit, separate from tests on purpose
      - run: pnpm test:unit -- --coverage
      - run: pnpm test:property
      - run: pnpm test:mutation --changed        # Stryker on changed files only
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: coverage, path: coverage/ }

  # ── Stage 2: integration. Parallel with stage 1 where the dependency graph allows.
  integration:
    name: Integration (Postgres, Redis)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16.4-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: test
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
          POSTGRES_DB: app_test
        ports: ['5432:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U test -d app_test"
          --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10
      redis:
        image: redis:7.4-alpine
        ports: ['6379:6379']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping" --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm test:integration
        env:
          TEST_DATABASE_URL: postgres://test:test@localhost:5432/app_test
          TEST_REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with: { name: integration-diagnostics, path: test-artifacts/ }

  # ── Stage 3: build once, reuse for E2E and preview deploy.
  build:
    needs: [verify]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      image: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.image }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm build
      - id: meta
        run: echo "image=ghcr.io/org/app:${{ github.sha }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  # ── Stage 4: E2E against a preview environment built from the PR artefact.
  e2e:
    needs: [build]
    if: contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'e2e') || github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false                        # keep siblings running: their traces are the evidence
      matrix:
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: pnpm exec playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
        env:
          E2E_BASE_URL: ${{ needs.deploy-preview.outputs.url }}
          RUN_ID: ${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with: { name: trace-${{ matrix.shard }}, path: e2e/.artifacts }

  # ── Stage 5: what blocks the merge.
  required:
    needs: [verify, integration, e2e]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: |
          echo "verify=${{ needs.verify.result }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "integration=${{ needs.integration.result }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "e2e=${{ needs.e2e.result }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: |
          test "${{ needs.verify.result }}" = "success"
          test "${{ needs.integration.result }}" = "success"
          if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" = "push" ]; then
            test "${{ needs.e2e.result }}" = "success"
          else
            echo "::notice::E2E is advisory on PRs; required on main."
          fi

  # ── Stage 6: nightly. The expensive matrix that must not gate every PR.
  nightly:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - run: pnpm exec playwright test --project=chromium --project=firefox --project=webkit --project=mobile-chrome
      - run: pnpm test:mutation
      - run: pnpm audit --audit-level=high
```

**Sharding mechanics and the mistake everyone makes.**

```bash
# Playwright shards by *file*, and --shard=n/total splits the file list.
# It does NOT balance by duration. A suite where one spec file takes 6 minutes
# and 40 files take 5 seconds each will have one shard that takes 6 minutes.
#
# Measure and rebalance:
npx playwright test --list                      # list all tests
npx playwright test --reporter=json > run.json   # per-test durations from the last run
node -e "                                        # greedy bin-packing by duration
  const r = require('./run.json');
  const shards = 4, bins = Array.from({length: shards}, () => ({d:0, files:new Set()}));
  const byFile = {};
  for (const s of r.suites.flatMap(s => s.specs)) {
    const f = s.file; (byFile[f] ||= []).push(s.tests[0]?.results?.[0]?.duration ?? 0);
  }
  for (const [f, ds] of Object.entries(byFile).sort((a,b) => b[1][0]-a[1][0])) {
    bins.sort((a,b) => a.d-b.d)[0].files.add(f); bins[0].d += ds.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
  }
  console.log(bins.map((b,i) => ({shard: i+1, files: b.files.size, seconds: Math.round(b.d/1000)})));
"
```

Other sharders and their behaviour:
- **Vitest/Jest**: `--shard=1/4` (Vitest) and `--shard=1/4` with `--sequence.shuffle` off; both split by file. Vitest also supports `--reporter=json` for the same duration analysis.
- **Cypress**: `--shard=1/4` (Cypress 10.7+), splitting by spec file; free.
- **K6**: no sharding; scale VUs per stage and run parallel processes with different `startTime`, or use k6 Cloud.

**Conditional execution: which tests run for which change.** The highest-leverage optimisation is not running the E2E suite for a documentation change.

```ts
// playwright.config.ts -- tag by area, and select by area in CI.
test('checkout', { tag: ['@checkout', '@money'] }, async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ })
test('about page', { tag: ['@content'] }, async ({ page }) => { /* ... */ })
```

```bash
# PR: run only the areas the diff touches. Labels come from a path->tag map in CI.
npx playwright test --grep-invert @content
# @smoke always runs, on every PR, in under 60 seconds.
npx playwright test --grep @smoke
```

**Test ordering by dependency and value.** Order your pipeline by `(value per second)`:

1. Lint + typecheck (seconds, catches 40% of mistakes)
2. Unit + property (seconds to a minute)
3. Integration (1-3 min)
4. Build (1-3 min, and every E2E test needs it)
5. E2E smoke (60s, on a cached environment)
6. Full E2E (5-10 min, parallel shards)
7. Nightly matrix (30-90 min, all browsers + mutation + audits)

Run 5 in parallel with 6 when possible. And **make the merge gate the union of the fast stages**, with full E2E required on `main` and advisory on PRs unless the change is user-facing.

**Caching that actually helps.**

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: |
      node_modules/.pnpm-store
      ~/.cache/ms-playwright
      ~/.cache/pnpm
    key: pnpm-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}-playwright-${{ hashFiles('playwright.config.ts') }}
    restore-keys: pnpm-${{ hashFiles('pnpm-lock.yaml') }}-
```

Cache: the pnpm store, the Playwright browser binaries, the Vite/Vitest transform cache, and the Stryker report directory. Do **not** cache `node_modules` with a native-addon-heavy tree, and never cache the test database.

**Trend and enforce.**

```yaml
- name: Fail if the flake rate exceeds the budget
  run: |
    npx playwright test --last-failed --reporter=json > retry.json || true
    node -e "
      const flaky = require('./retry.json').suites.flatMap(s=>s.specs).filter(s => s.tests.some(t => t.results.length > 1));
      const total  = require('./retry.json').suites.flatMap(s=>s.specs).length;
      const rate = (flaky.length / total) * 100;
      console.log('flake rate: ' + rate.toFixed(2) + '%');
      if (rate > 0.5) { console.error('::error::Flake budget exceeded'); process.exit(1); }
    "
```

**Trade-offs.**

- **More stages = better feedback latency but more pipeline complexity** and more places for a status badge to lie. Four or five well-defined stages beat ten.
- **A preview environment per PR is the best fidelity and the slowest.** Cache aggressively; reuse environments per branch; deploy only when the build or migrations change.
- **Advisory vs required E2E on PRs** is a genuine political decision. Required gives confidence and costs developer time; advisory gives speed and lets regressions reach main. The pragmatic answer: required for user-facing changes (label-driven), advisory otherwise, always required on main.
- **Sharding by file is a blunt instrument.** Unbalanced suites need either rebalancing by file or splitting the long specs.
- **Fail-fast cancels useful work.** Always `fail-fast: false` in a test matrix.
- **A "required" aggregator job** is often worth it, because branch protection cannot express "these 3 of 5 jobs are required, and E2E only on main" cleanly.

**Common mistakes.**

1. Running everything on every PR, so the pipeline takes 40 minutes and developers batch their work.
2. `fail-fast: true` on a test matrix, cancelling the shards that were about to fail and whose traces you needed.
3. Sharding 4 ways when the suite is 90 seconds; the coordination overhead exceeds the gain.
4. Uploading traces only on the aggregated result, losing the per-shard evidence.
5. Reinstalling Playwright browsers on every job instead of caching them.
6. No `concurrency` group, so five pushes to a branch queue five 30-minute pipelines.
7. Marking a test "pending" or "skip" in the PR to make CI green, with no follow-up.
8. Treating a green `main` E2E run as optional because "the deploy smoke test passed" -- the deploy smoke test only covers 3 journeys.
9. Not measuring which tests are the slowest, so the shard imbalance persists for years.
10. No flake-rate metric, so the suite silently decays from 0.2% to 8% and nobody notices until a release is blocked.

**Interviewer probes.**

- 🟢 *"How do you structure a CI testing pipeline?"* -- Ordered by value per second: lint/types, unit/property, integration with real services, build, E2E smoke, full E2E sharded, and a nightly matrix. Only the fast stages gate the merge; the expensive ones gate main and releases.
- 🟡 *"What is test sharding and what is the mistake people make?"* -- Splitting the suite into N groups to run in parallel. The mistake is assuming it balances: most sharders split by file count, not by duration, so one slow spec makes one shard five times longer. Measure per-test durations and rebalance.
- 🔴 *"CI is 45 minutes. Walk me through reducing it."* -- (1) Measure where the time goes per stage. (2) Cut what does not need to gate: docs/lint-only changes skip E2E. (3) Parallelise the unit and integration stages. (4) Shard E2E 4-6 ways with `fail-fast: false`. (5) Cache the pnpm store and Playwright browsers. (6) Reuse the preview environment per branch instead of deploying per run. (7) Make full E2E advisory on PRs, required on main. (8) Split the slowest spec files.
- 🔴 *"How do you know your test suite is healthy?"* -- Five numbers, tracked over time: unit suite duration, integration duration, E2E wall clock, flake rate (tests that failed then passed on retry), and quarantine size. Plus the ratio of E2E to total tests, and the defect-escape rate by tier (which bugs got past which tier). If flake rate trends up, quality is down even if everything is green.
- ⚫ *"How would you require E2E on PRs that touch the checkout but not on a README change?"* -- Path or label based selection. Either a label (`e2e`) applied by a bot from the diff paths, or a `tags`/`grep` selector computed in CI from the changed-file list, with the `required` aggregator job reading the job result conditionally. Either way, the rule must be visible in the PR so nobody is surprised by a 10-minute pipeline.

---
